claims.claim: 300 worker processes at 60–100 MB each is 18–30 GB of containers, mostly idle and waiting on the network
claims.measured: python-flask peak memory 117–123 MB per container (115 MB idle); 18% CPU in the 10 ms I/O-wait test
claims.why: Each sync Flask container measured about 115–123 MB, within a factor of 2 of 60–100 MB per worker, and it sat mostly idle (18% CPU) while waiting on I/O.

claims.claim: gunicorn gthread workers (e.g. 8 processes × 32 threads) are the first choice for the capacity problem because threads release the GIL during network waits
claims.measured: I/O wait: gthread 374 rps (p50 678 ms, 19% CPU) vs sync flask 276 rps vs gevent 2,956 rps
claims.why: The benchmark doesn't give the thread count it used, and its gthread setup gained only about 1.35× over sync under I/O wait, so the proposed 8×32 configuration can't be checked against it.

claims.claim: gevent workers are viable and efficient
claims.measured: I/O wait: gevent 2,956 rps vs sync flask 276 rps and gthread 374 rps
claims.why: Under the I/O-wait load, gevent handled about 8–10× the throughput of the sync and gthread Flask servers.

claims.claim: Scaling out sync workers works but is expensive and fragile when the insurer slows down
claims.measured: I/O wait: 276 rps, p50 915 ms, 18% CPU, 122 MB per container
claims.why: A sync Flask container managed only 276 rps under a 10 ms wait while using 122 MB and leaving most of its CPU idle, so you would need many containers.
